messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 49-year-old architect, a man who spends his days designing spaces meant to feel safe and functional. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, after months of what she called “living like a cornered animal.” He could not argue with her. The trouble began two years ago, when he was walking home from a client meeting in a downtown commercial district. He turned a corner and saw a man being beaten against the side of a dumpster—a chaotic, brutal scene that lasted only seconds before the attacker fled, but which seemed to stretch into an endless loop in his mind. David did not know the victim; he called 911 and waited for the ambulance, but the image of the man’s head hitting the metal, the wet sound, the smell of garbage and blood, stayed with him. He could not put the memory in order. He knew what happened, but when he tried to tell his wife that night, he could not find the words. Instead, he felt the event happening right now—his heart pounding, his palms sweating, the nausea rising in his throat. He had come to believe there was something about him that made the event happen, as if his presence had somehow invited the violence, and he was certain he could not stop bad things from happening to him.

In the weeks that followed, David began to notice that certain smells—the metallic tang of a trash can, the sour odor of a city alley—would send a wave of nausea through him, and the nausea would trigger a sudden, vivid reliving of the event. He would be standing in his own kitchen, and the smell of a ripe banana peel would flash him back to the dumpster, and then he felt the fear all over again. That fear made him feel jumpy, easily startled, and he found himself scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room or building. He felt unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the entire room. The violence he had witnessed had become a kind of template: every loud noise, every sudden movement on the street, felt like a prelude to another attack. He began to avoid driving past that block, then the whole neighborhood, then any area with dumpsters visible from the road. This avoidance meant he took longer routes to work, arriving late to meetings, and he stopped going to the firm’s annual happy hour because the bar was near a loading dock. He felt isolated and set apart from others, convinced that no one could understand what he had seen, and that he was somehow marked by it.

His own sense of helplessness deepened the problem. He was certain he could not stop bad things from happening, so he began to monitor the world for signs of danger, and that monitoring itself became a trigger. He would see a group of men standing too close together on a sidewalk, and the sight of potential violence would make him nauseous, which would pull him back into the memory, which would make him scan the exits again. The loop tightened. The more he scanned, the more he saw threats; the more he saw threats, the more he relived the event; the more he relived it, the more convinced he became that his own intrinsic fault had drawn him to that corner at that moment. He started to feel unsafe in his own home, sitting with his back to the kitchen, and he rearranged the furniture in his study so that his desk faced the door. His wife found him standing in the doorway of their bedroom at night, checking the lock three times before he could lie down.

What finally brought David to therapy was not the fear itself, but the isolation. He had stopped accepting invitations from friends, stopped attending his son’s basketball games because the gym had too many exits and too many people. He was becoming a stranger to his own family, and he was afraid that if he did not find a way out of this cycle, he would lose them entirely. He hoped someone could help him find the words he had lost, and the order he could not remember.
